questions.text: Q2.4: Compute the DFT of a 2 × 2 image with values `[1 2; 3 4]`, then interpret the frequency components.

steps.text: 2-D DFT: `F(u,v) = Σx Σy f(x,y)·e^(−j2π(ux/M + vy/N))`. For M = N = 2 the exponential is just (−1)^(ux + vy), with x the row and y the column.
`F(0,1) = (1 + 3) − (2 + 4) = −2` (left column minus right column)
`F(1,0) = (1 + 2) − (3 + 4) = −4` (top row minus bottom row)
`F(1,1) = 1 − 2 − 3 + 4 = 0` (the diagonal, checkerboard pattern)
Result without scaling (MATLAB's fft2):
With the lecture's 1/MN = 1/4 in the forward transform:
F(0,0) is the DC term: the total brightness (with 1/MN, the mean 2.5). It is by far the largest coefficient.

F(1,0) = −4 is the vertical variation: values grow by 2 from the top row to the bottom row. F(0,1) = −2 is the horizontal variation: values grow by 1 from left to right, so the vertical change is twice as strong. The minus signs mean the values increase (rather than decrease) along that direction.
F(1,1) = 0: there is no checkerboard (diagonal) pattern, since 1 + 4 = 2 + 3. All the coefficients are real because every exponential of a 2 × 2 DFT is ±1; the magnitude spectrum is [10 2; 4 0].

questions.answer: F = [10 −2; −4 0] without scaling (MATLAB's fft2), or [2.5 −0.5; −1 0] with the lecture's 1/MN factor. DC dominates, the vertical change (−4) is twice the horizontal one (−2), and there is no diagonal component (0).
questions.why: The paper does not fix where the 1/MN factor goes. The lecture pages put it in the forward transform (giving [2.5 −0.5; −1 0]); MATLAB's fft2 and Gonzalez put it in the inverse (giving [10 −2; −4 0]). Both are shown.

questions.text: Q1A: What are the applications of image processing? (Give a short description of each.)

steps.text: Medical imaging: enhancing X-ray, CT and MRI images, detecting tumours, measuring organs, classifying chest X-rays (e.g. for COVID-19).
Surveillance (CCTV): real-time monitoring, counting people, detecting crowds and abnormal behaviour.
Traffic: automatic number plate recognition (ANPR) for gates, tolls and vehicle tracking.
Self-driving cars and robots: detecting lanes, traffic lights, signs and obstacles, even in fog.
Industrial inspection: checking and sorting products, rejecting faulty or unlabelled items on a conveyor belt.
Remote sensing and astronomy: enhancing satellite and telescope images for maps, weather, crops and land use.
Documents and biometrics: scanning and reading text (OCR), fingerprint, iris and face recognition.
Photography and media: removing noise, sharpening, adjusting brightness, contrast and colour, compressing images for storage and transmission.

questions.text: Q1B, step 1 of 2: the 3×3 neighbourhood of the marked pixel (177) in the original image is shown. What value does the 3×3 min filter give the marked pixel?
questions.why: A min filter (rank-order filter) returns the smallest of the 9 values {100, 210, 203, 167, 177, 48, 44, 81, 125}, which is 44. 125 is the median and 210 the maximum.
questions.ref: Midterm Nov 2022 · Q1B step 1 · solved here

questions.text: Q1B, step 2 of 2: after the min filter, the 3×3 values around the marked pixel are shown. What does the vertical Sobel mask `[-1 0 1; -2 0 2; -1 0 1]` give at the marked pixel (mask laid directly on the image)?
questions.why: (−25 + 25) + 2(−9 + 41) + (−9 + 30) = 0 + 64 + 21 = 85. 27 is the horizontal mask `[-1 -2 -1; 0 0 0; 1 2 1]` (the book's Gy, which detects horizontal edges), −54 is Sobel on the original without the min filter, and 53 forgets the weight 2 of the middle row.
questions.ref: Midterm Nov 2022 · Q1B step 2 · solved here

questions.text: Q1B: The image below is filtered by a 3×3 min filter. After that the image is filtered by a vertical 3×3 Sobel filter. What is the result at the marked pixel (177, row 5, column 5, shown in brackets)?

steps.text: The Sobel mask at the marked pixel needs the min-filtered values of rows 4–6, columns 4–6, and each of those needs a 3×3 window of the original, so only rows 3–7 and columns 3–7 are used. No border pixel is involved, so padding does not matter.

Min filter: replace each of these 9 pixels by the smallest value in its own 3×3 window. For the marked pixel the window {100, 210, 203, 167, 177, 48, 44, 81, 125} gives 44; the top row gets 25 three times (the 25 at row 3, column 5 lies in all three windows).
The vertical Sobel mask (the course book's Gx, which detects vertical edges) is `[-1 0 1; -2 0 2; -1 0 1]`: right column minus left column, with the middle row weighted by 2.
With true convolution the mask is first rotated by 180°, which only flips the sign (−85); the edge strength |85| is the same.

questions.answer: 85 (−85 if the mask is convolved, i.e. rotated by 180°; the magnitude is 85).
questions.why: The paper does not print the mask. 'Vertical Sobel' is taken as the course book's Gx = `[-1 0 1; -2 0 2; -1 0 1]`, which the book (Ch 3 p. 75) says detects vertical edges; the same examiner's Nov 2023 key also names `[-1 -2 -1; 0 0 0; 1 2 1]` 'Sobel (horizontal)'. Texts that call `[-1 -2 -1; 0 0 0; 1 2 1]` the vertical mask get 27 instead.

questions.text: Q2, step 1 of 2: for the 64×64, 3-bit image (MN = 4096) with n_k = 790, 1023, 850, 656, 329, 245, 122, 81 for levels 0–7, what is the equalized value s_2?
questions.why: Cumulative count up to level 2 is 790 + 1023 + 850 = 2663; s_2 = 7 × 2663 / 4096 = 4.55, which rounds to 5. Truncating gives 4, and 7 × 850 / 4096 = 1.45 → 1 forgets to cumulate.
questions.ref: Midterm Nov 2022 · Q2 step 1 · solved here

questions.text: Q2, step 2 of 2: after equalization, how many pixels have the new grey level 6?
questions.why: Level 3 gives 7 × 3319 / 4096 = 5.67 → 6 and level 4 gives 7 × 3648 / 4096 = 6.23 → 6, so both bars merge: 656 + 329 = 985. 448 is the merged count at level 7 (245 + 122 + 81).
questions.ref: Midterm Nov 2022 · Q2 step 2 · solved here

questions.text: Q2: Suppose that a 3-bit image (L = 8) of size 64 × 64 pixels (MN = 4096) has the intensity distribution shown in the following table, where the intensity levels are integers in the range [0, L − 1] = [0, 7]. 1. Get the transformation function. 2. Get the histogram equalization.

steps.text: Normalize: p_r(r_k) = n_k / MN with MN = 4096 (the counts add up to 4096).
Transformation function: s_k = T(r_k) = (L − 1) × Σ p_r(r_j) for j = 0..k, i.e. 7 × (cumulative count) / 4096, rounded to the nearest integer.
Equalized histogram: add the counts of the old levels that map to the same new level; levels 0, 2 and 4 end up empty.
Only 5 distinct levels remain: the histogram now spreads over the whole range but is not perfectly flat, because equalization can merge bars but never split them.

questions.why: The scanned table is overexposed. The counts are read as 790, 1023, 850, 656, 329, 245, 122, 81 (the textbook example with this exact wording): they match the visible number of digits in each row and add up to MN = 4096.

questions.text: Q3A, step 1 of 2: f = 0 0 0 1 0 0 0 0 is a discrete unit impulse and w = 1 2 4 2 8. What does correlating w with f produce around the impulse?
questions.why: In correlation w slides unrotated, and since f is a single 1 each output equals the mask value lying on the 1, so w comes out reversed: full result 0 0 0 8 2 4 2 1 0 0 0 0.
questions.ref: Midterm Nov 2022 · Q3A step 1 · solved here

questions.text: Q3A, step 2 of 2: what is the convolution of w = 1 2 4 2 8 with the impulse f = 0 0 0 1 0 0 0 0, cropped to the 8 samples of f?
questions.why: Convolution rotates w by 180° first, which cancels the reversal, so the impulse reproduces w with its centre (4) on the impulse position: 0 1 2 4 2 8 0 0. 0 8 2 4 2 1 0 0 is the cropped correlation.
questions.ref: Midterm Nov 2022 · Q3A step 2 · solved here

questions.text: Q3A: Compute the 1-D correlation and convolution of a filter w with a discrete unit impulse f (origin at the first sample of f).

steps.text: The mask has m = 5 values, so pad f with m − 1 = 4 zeros on each side; then every shift of w overlaps f.
Correlation: slide w (not rotated) along the padded f; at each shift multiply and add. Only the sample under the 1 counts, so the output is w read backwards.
Convolution: rotate w by 180° (8 2 4 2 1) and repeat; now the output is w in its original order.
Cropped to the size of f (drop 2 samples at each end): correlation 0 8 2 4 2 1 0 0, convolution 0 1 2 4 2 8 0 0.
Conclusion: correlating a function with a unit impulse gives a 180°-rotated copy of the function; convolving reproduces it exactly, which is why convolution with an impulse copies the filter.

questions.why: The mask is printed very small and is read as 1 2 4 2 8 (the textbook version of this example uses 1 2 3 2 8). Either way correlation gives the mask reversed and convolution gives it unchanged.

questions.text: Q3B: What are the types of filter used to enhance Fig. 1, Fig. 2 and Fig. 3? (Fig. 1: a portrait covered with fine, grainy noise over every pixel. Fig. 2: a baboon face sprinkled with many isolated bright specks. Fig. 3: a dark MRI scan of a head shown next to a light version in which dark and bright are swapped.)

steps.text: Fig. 1 (fine grainy noise on every pixel, like Gaussian noise): a smoothing low-pass filter, the averaging (mean) filter or a Gaussian filter, which averages the noise out at the cost of a little blur.

Fig. 2 (isolated specks, i.e. salt-and-pepper impulse noise): the median filter. The impulses fall at the ends of the sorted window and are never chosen, so the noise disappears and edges stay sharp; averaging would only smear the specks into grey blotches.

Fig. 3 (a dark MRI and its negative): the image negative (complement), the point operation s = (L − 1) − r, i.e. 255 − r for 8 bits. It turns the dark scan into a light one, so grey detail embedded in large dark regions is easier to see.
In short: Fig. 1 → mean or Gaussian smoothing, Fig. 2 → median filter, Fig. 3 → negative (complement) transformation.

questions.why: Fig. 3 is read as a before/after pair (original and its negative). If the examiner meant the MRI to be enhanced in some other way, contrast stretching or sharpening would also be defensible.

questions.text: Q1.1: Which of the following is used to resolve the dark features in the image?
questions.why: A power-law (gamma) transformation with γ < 1 expands the dark grey levels and brightens the image, revealing detail in dark regions. Gaussian and Laplacian are smoothing and edge filters, and histogram specification needs a target histogram to be chosen.
questions.ref: Midterm Nov 2023 · Q1.1 · from the key

questions.text: Q1.2: What is the output of a smoothing, linear spatial filter?
questions.why: A linear smoothing (averaging) filter outputs the average of the pixels under the mask. Maximum, minimum and median are non-linear order-statistic (rank) filters.
questions.ref: Midterm Nov 2023 · Q1.2 · from the key

questions.text: Q1.3: Which is a color attribute that describes a pure color?
questions.why: Hue is the dominant colour itself (pure red, yellow, ...), which the course book (Ch 1 p. 20) calls the colour type. Saturation, which the book calls the purity of the colour, measures how far that pure colour is diluted with white (how pure it is, not which colour it is), and brightness/intensity are the achromatic amount of light.
questions.ref: Midterm Nov 2023 · Q1.3 · from the key

questions.text: Q1.4: ...... represents the transition between image function's continuous values and its digital equivalent.
questions.why: Quantization digitizes the amplitude: continuous grey values become a finite set of levels. Sampling digitizes the coordinates (positions), not the values.
questions.ref: Midterm Nov 2023 · Q1.4 · from the key

questions.text: Q1.5: While performing the median filtering, suppose a 3*3 neighborhood has value (10, 20, 20, 20, 15, 20, 20, 25, 100), then what is the median value to be given to the pixel under filter?
questions.why: Sorted: 10, 15, 20, 20, 20, 20, 20, 25, 100; the median is the 5th of 9 values, 20. The outlier 100 is ignored.
questions.ref: Midterm Nov 2023 · Q1.5 · from the key

questions.text: Q2a, step 1 of 1: the image is brightened by multiplying every pixel by 2 (the reverse of the slide's divide-by-2 example). What does the pixel 200 become in an 8-bit image?
questions.why: 2 × 200 = 400 is above 255, so it is clipped to 255. 400 forgets clipping, 144 is the uint8 wrap-around (400 − 256), and 100 is the divide-by-2 (darkening) result.
questions.ref: Midterm Nov 2023 · Q2a step 1 · solved here

questions.text: Q2a: Apply the method to change the brightness of the image into a brighter image.

steps.text: Brightness is changed by a point operation g(x, y) = T(f(x, y)) applied to each pixel on its own. The slide's example uses T = divide by 2, which gives the darker image 3 4 1 0 / 6 100 10 5.
To brighten, multiply by a constant greater than 1 (here 2) or add a positive constant.
g = 2f gives 12 16 4 0 / 24 400 40 20; round and clip to 0–255, so 400 becomes 255.
Alternative: g = f + 50 gives 56 58 52 50 / 62 250 70 60 (no clipping needed here).
Multiplying also stretches the grey levels apart (more contrast); adding shifts them all up and keeps the differences.

questions.why: The paper does not fix the operator; the key only points to the slide's divide-by-2 example, so its reverse (multiply by 2) is used here. Adding a constant, or a log or gamma < 1 transform, are also accepted ways to brighten.

questions.text: Q2b, step 1 of 2: with the Laplacian mask `[0 1 0; 1 -4 1; 0 1 0]`, what is the second derivative at the shaded pixel in row 2, column 2?
questions.why: Up 20 + down 10 + left 20 + right 10 − 4 × 10 = 60 − 40 = 20. 60 forgets the −4 × centre term.
questions.ref: Midterm Nov 2023 · Q2b step 1 · from the key

questions.text: Q2b, step 2 of 2: what is the second derivative at the shaded pixel in row 3, column 3?
questions.why: All four neighbours are 10: 10 + 10 + 10 + 10 − 4 × 10 = 0. Inside a flat region the Laplacian (a sum-zero, high-pass mask) is 0.
questions.ref: Midterm Nov 2023 · Q2b step 2 · from the key

questions.text: Q2b: Find the second derivative for the shaded pixels (row 2, column 2 and row 3, column 3, shown in brackets).

steps.text: The 2-D second derivative is the Laplacian: ∇²f = f(x + 1, y) + f(x − 1, y) + f(x, y + 1) + f(x, y − 1) − 4f(x, y), i.e. the mask `[0 1 0; 1 -4 1; 0 1 0]`.
Row 2, column 2 (value 10): neighbours 20 (up), 10 (down), 20 (left), 10 (right): 20 + 10 + 20 + 10 − 4 × 10 = 20.
Row 3, column 3 (value 10): all four neighbours are 10: 10 + 10 + 10 + 10 − 4 × 10 = 0.
The pixel on the corner of the step between the 20s and the 10s responds; the pixel inside the flat region of 10s gives 0, as a sum-zero high-pass mask should.

questions.answer: ∇²f = 20 at row 2, column 2 and ∇²f = 0 at row 3, column 3.
questions.ref: Midterm Nov 2023 · Q2b · from the key

questions.text: Q2c: Write the name of the filter for each mask.

steps.text: Mask 1 `[-1 -1 -1; -1 8 -1; -1 -1 -1]`: Laplacian (the 8-neighbour version, the negative of `[1 1 1; 1 -8 1; 1 1 1]`). Its coefficients add up to 0, so it is a high-pass edge detector.
Mask 2 `[-1 -1 -1; -1 17 -1; -1 -1 -1]`: high-boost filter. The centre is w = 9A − 1, so 17 means A = 2: the high-pass detail plus (A − 1) = 1 times the original.
Mask 3 `[-1 -2 -1; 0 0 0; 1 2 1]`: Sobel (horizontal). It subtracts the row above from the row below, with the middle column weighted by 2, so it detects horizontal edges.

questions.ref: Midterm Nov 2023 · Q2c · from the key

questions.text: Q3, step 1 of 2: in the 4×8, 3-bit image (every row is 0 1 1 2 2 3 4 4), what does grey level 2 map to after histogram equalization?
questions.why: Counts: 4, 8, 8 for levels 0–2, so the cumulative count is 20; 7 × 20 / 32 = 4.375 → 4. 5 comes from using L = 8 instead of L − 1 = 7 (8 × 20 / 32), and 2 from forgetting to cumulate (7 × 8 / 32 = 1.75).
questions.ref: Midterm Nov 2023 · Q3 step 1 · solved here

questions.text: Q3, step 2 of 2: what does grey level 3 map to?
questions.why: Cumulative count up to level 3 is 4 + 8 + 8 + 4 = 24; 7 × 24 / 32 = 5.25 → 5. 6 uses L instead of L − 1 (8 × 24 / 32), and 1 forgets to cumulate (7 × 4 / 32 = 0.875).
questions.ref: Midterm Nov 2023 · Q3 step 2 · solved here

questions.text: Q3: Suppose that a 3-bit image of size 4 × 8 pixels (MN = 32), (L = 8), where the intensity levels are integers in the range [0, L − 1] = [0, 7]. Get the histogram equalization.

steps.text: Count the grey levels: every row is 0 1 1 2 2 3 4 4, so level 0 has 4 pixels, 1 has 8, 2 has 8, 3 has 4, 4 has 8 and levels 5–7 have none (total 32).
s_k = round((L − 1) × cumulative / MN) = round(7 × cum / 32).
Apply the mapping to every pixel.
New histogram: 4 pixels at 1, 8 at 3, 8 at 4, 4 at 5 and 8 at 7; the bars keep their heights but are spread over 1–7 instead of 0–4.

questions.answer: 0→1, 1→3, 2→4, 3→5, 4→7; every row of the output image is 1 3 3 4 4 5 7 7.

questions.text: Q1.1: Piecewise linear transformation provides flexibility for mapping intensity ranges.
questions.why: Each straight piece can have its own slope, so any band of grey levels can be stretched (slope > 1) or compressed (slope < 1) independently.

questions.text: Q1.2: Replication padding replaces edge pixels with the nearest border value.
questions.why: Replicate padding fills the pixels added outside the image with a copy of the nearest border pixel, so the intended answer is True. Strictly, the image's own edge pixels are kept; it is the new padding pixels that take the border value.

questions.text: Q1.3: Adding a constant to pixel intensity changes image contrast.
questions.why: False: adding a constant shifts every grey level by the same amount, which changes brightness but keeps the differences between pixels (except where values are clipped at 0 or 255). Multiplying by a constant changes contrast.

questions.text: Q1.4: The histogram of a high-contrast image covers a wide range of intensity values.
questions.why: A high-contrast image uses most of the grey scale, so its histogram is spread over a wide range; a low-contrast image has a narrow histogram.

questions.text: Q1.5: In brightness adjustment, adding a negative constant makes the image darker.
questions.why: Adding a negative constant (subtracting) lowers every grey value, with negative results clipped to 0, so the image becomes darker.

questions.text: Q1.6: Image processing is only used for image enhancement.
questions.why: False: besides enhancement, image processing covers restoration, segmentation, compression, feature extraction and preparing images for machine perception (computer vision).

questions.text: Q2.1: Laplacian is a ......
questions.why: The Laplacian is the sum of the second derivatives in x and y, ∇²f = ∂²f/∂x² + ∂²f/∂y²; Sobel is a first-order (gradient) operator.

questions.text: Q2.2: Which mathematical operation is typically used in linear spatial filtering?
questions.why: A linear spatial filter slides a mask over the image and takes a weighted sum at each position: convolution (or correlation). The Fourier transform belongs to frequency-domain filtering.

questions.text: Q2.3: Which statement correctly differentiates image processing from computer vision?
options: Image processing focuses on hardware design while computer vision deals with photography
Image processing extracts knowledge, computer vision enhances images
Image processing enhances and analyzes images, while computer vision interprets and understands them
There is no difference between them
questions.why: Image processing takes an image and produces an improved or transformed image; computer vision takes an image and produces understanding (objects, events, decisions).

questions.text: Q2.4: What is the difference between Convolution and Correlation?
options: Image is pre-rotated by 180 degree for Correlation
Image is pre-rotated by 180 degree for Convolution
Image is pre-rotated by 90 degree for Correlation
Image is pre-rotated by 90 degree for Convolution
questions.why: Convolution rotates one operand by 180° before sliding and correlation rotates nothing. The lecture rotates the mask, but convolution is commutative, so rotating the image instead is the same operation: B is the intended answer.

questions.text: Q2.5: What happens when the bit depth of a grayscale image increases?
options: The number of possible gray levels decreases
The number of gray levels increases, improving image detail
questions.why: With k bits a pixel can take 2^k grey levels, so more bits give more levels, finer tonal detail and less false contouring (but a larger file).

questions.text: Q2.6: Which of the following is an advantage of point processing?
options: It considers spatial relationships of pixels
It is computationally fast and simple
It provides noise reduction and edge detection
questions.why: A point operation computes each output pixel from that pixel's value alone (often a look-up table), so it is fast and simple; neighbourhood operations are needed for noise reduction, edges and texture.

questions.text: Q2.7: To prevent overflow, pixel values must be ......
questions.why: After arithmetic, results above 255 (or below 0) are clipped to the 8-bit range 0–255. Computing in float avoids wrap-around during the calculation, but the result must still be clipped to be stored as 8 bits.

questions.text: Q2.8: Zero padding in spatial filtering refers to: ......
options: Setting missing edge pixels to zero
Replacing all pixel values with zeros
questions.why: Near the border the mask falls outside the image; zero padding fills those missing neighbours with 0 so the output keeps the input size (at the cost of dark border artefacts). Ignoring the border is the no-padding (cropping) option.

questions.text: Q2.9: Which of the following is the disadvantage of a smoothing filter?
questions.why: Averaging removes noise but also smooths the sharp grey-level transitions at edges, so edges become blurred; that is the price of smoothing.

questions.text: Q2.10: To convert a continuous sensed data into Digital form, which of the following is required?
questions.why: Digitizing needs both: sampling digitizes the coordinates and quantization digitizes the amplitude (grey values).

questions.text: Q3a: Complete the following diagram: the basic intensity-transformation curves. The diagram plots output level s against input level r (both from 0 to L − 1) with six unlabelled curves: a falling straight line, the rising diagonal, two curves above the diagonal (one rising very steeply at first) and two below it (one staying flat until near the end). Label each curve.

steps.text: Falling straight line from (0, L − 1) to (L − 1, 0): negative, `s = L − 1 − r`.
Rising diagonal: identity, `s = r` (no change).
Steepest curve above the diagonal (shoots up, then flattens): log, `s = c·log(1 + r)`.
Curve between the log curve and the diagonal: nth root, i.e. power law `s = c·r^γ` with γ < 1.
Curve just below the diagonal: nth power, i.e. power law with γ > 1.
Lowest curve (flat almost to the end, then rising sharply): inverse log (exponential).
Curves above the diagonal expand the dark levels and brighten the image; curves below expand the bright levels and darken it.

questions.text: Q3b: Describe the type of contrast problem based on the following histograms: (1, top left) bars crowded at the low end; (2, top right) bars crowded at the high end; (3, bottom left) a narrow cluster of bars in the middle; (4, bottom right) bars spread fairly evenly over the whole range.

steps.text: (1) Dark image: most pixels have low grey levels and the bright part of the range is unused.
(2) Bright (light) image: most pixels have high grey levels and the dark part of the range is unused.
(3) Low-contrast image: the grey levels occupy only a narrow band, so the image looks dull and washed out; contrast stretching or histogram equalization fixes it.
(4) High-contrast (good) image: the histogram covers the whole grey scale fairly uniformly, so no contrast correction is needed.

questions.text: Q1, step 1 of 2: for the 3-bit 4×4 image below, what does grey level 4 map to after histogram equalization?
questions.why: Counts: level 1 has 1 pixel, 3 has 6, 4 has 5, 5 has 4; cumulative up to 4 is 1 + 6 + 5 = 12, and 7 × 12 / 16 = 5.25 → 5. 6 uses L = 8 instead of 7, and 2 forgets to cumulate (7 × 5 / 16 = 2.19).

questions.text: Q1, step 2 of 2: what does the single pixel with grey level 1 become?

questions.text: Q1: Suppose that you have been given the 3-bit 4×4 image shown below. Show the output image as a result of histogram equalization. (Show all your steps.)

steps.text: L = 2³ = 8 levels and MN = 4 × 4 = 16 pixels; p_r(r_k) = n_k / 16.
s_k = T(r_k) = (L − 1) × Σ p_r(r_j) = 7 × (cumulative count) / 16, rounded.
Mapping of the levels present: 1 → 0, 3 → 3, 4 → 5, 5 → 7.
Replace every pixel by its new level.
New histogram: 1 pixel at 0, 6 at 3, 5 at 5, 4 at 7 (p = 1/16, 6/16, 5/16, 4/16): the same bars, spread over 0–7.

questions.text: Q2, step 1 of 3: the transformation is `s = α·log₂(1 + r) + β`. The input pixels 3 and 15 become 5 and 11. What are α and β?
questions.why: log₂(1 + 3) = 2 and log₂(1 + 15) = 4, so 2α + β = 5 and 4α + β = 11. Subtracting gives 2α = 6, α = 3, and β = 5 − 6 = −1.

questions.text: Q2, step 2 of 3: with `s = 3·log₂(1 + r) − 1`, what is the output pixel marked '?' (its input is 1)?
questions.why: s = 3·log₂(1 + 1) − 1 = 3 × 1 − 1 = 2. 3 forgets β, and −1 uses log₂(r) instead of log₂(1 + r).
questions.ref: Quiz 1 Nov 2024 (InfoSec) · Q2 step 2 · from the key

questions.text: Q2, step 3 of 3: what is the input pixel marked '?' (its output is 8)?
questions.why: 8 = 3·log₂(1 + r) − 1, so log₂(1 + r) = 3, 1 + r = 2³ = 8 and r = 7. 8 is 1 + r, not r; 3 is the logarithm itself.
questions.ref: Quiz 1 Nov 2024 (InfoSec) · Q2 step 3 · from the key

questions.text: Q2: A 4×4, 4 bits/pixel image passes through a point-wise intensity transformation given by `s = T(r) = α·log₂(1 + r) + β`, where α and β are unknown parameters. Only a few pixels are available in the input and output images, as shown below (– = not given). (a) Find α and β. (b) What's the value of the pixel with the '?' mark in the output image? (c) What's the value of the pixel with the '?' mark in the input image?

steps.text: Matching positions give the pairs r = 3 → s = 5, r = 15 → s = 11 and again r = 3 → s = 5.
(a) (2) − (1): 2α = 6, so α = 3; then β = 5 − 2 × 3 = −1. The transformation is `s = 3·log₂(1 + r) − 1`.
(b) The output '?' sits where the input is 1: s = 3·log₂(2) − 1 = 3 − 1 = 2.
(c) The input '?' sits where the output is 8: 3·log₂(1 + r) = 9, log₂(1 + r) = 3, 1 + r = 8, so r = 7.

questions.answer: α = 3, β = −1; the output '?' is 2; the input '?' is 7.
questions.ref: Quiz 1 Nov 2024 (InfoSec) · Q2 · from the key

Unlike equalization, the spacing stays proportional: equal steps in r stay equal steps in s.

questions.text: Which filter is primarily used for image smoothing by averaging neighboring pixel values?
questions.why: The mean (averaging) filter replaces each pixel by the plain average of its neighbourhood. The Gaussian also smooths but with unequal weights, and the Laplacian and Sobel filters find edges.

questions.text: Which of the following is an advantage of point processing?
options: It is computationally fast and simple
It considers spatial relationships of pixels
It provides noise reduction and edge detection
questions.why: Each output pixel depends only on its own value, so the whole operation is one lookup-table pass. Spatial relationships, textures, noise removal and edges need neighbourhood processing.

questions.text: Zero padding in spatial filtering refers to:
options: Setting missing edge pixels to zero
Replacing all pixel values with zeros
questions.why: When the mask hangs over the border, the missing neighbours outside the image are taken as 0. Ignoring the border pixels is the no-padding option, which shrinks the output.

questions.text: To prevent overflow, pixel values must be ......
questions.why: After arithmetic, results above 255 are set to 255 and results below 0 are set to 0 (clipping), so an 8-bit image never wraps around.
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model1-4 · from the key

questions.text: An image is represented digitally as a ......
questions.why: A digital grey image is a 2-D function f(x, y) stored as a matrix: each element (pixel) holds the intensity at that position.
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model1-5 · from the key

questions.text: Which mathematical operation is typically used in linear spatial filtering?
questions.why: Linear spatial filtering slides a mask over the image and takes the sum of products at each position, which is convolution (correlation when the mask is not rotated by 180°).
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model1-6 · from the key

questions.text: How could sampling be defined for a continuous image f(x, y)?
questions.why: Sampling digitizes the coordinates (x, y). Digitizing the amplitude (intensity) values is quantization.
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model1-7 · from the key

questions.text: Brightness adjustment can be achieved by adding or subtracting a constant value to pixel intensities.
questions.why: `y = x + C` brightens and `y = x − C` darkens every pixel by the same amount, with clipping to 0–255.

The manipulation and analysis of digital images to enhance quality or extract information

questions.text: Piecewise linear transformation is mainly used for ......
questions.why: The user chooses the breakpoints, so any grey range can be stretched or compressed, which makes it a flexible contrast-enhancement tool.
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model2-4 · solved here

questions.text: What is the purpose of gamma correction?
options: To reduce noise in the image
questions.why: `s = c·r^γ` bends the grey-level curve: γ < 1 brightens the dark range and γ > 1 darkens; it is also used to correct images for display on monitors.
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model2-5 · solved here

questions.text: Image filtering in the spatial domain modifies pixel values by ......
questions.why: Spatial-domain methods work on the pixels themselves at their (x, y) positions. Multiplying frequencies is filtering in the frequency domain.
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model2-6 · solved here

questions.text: Which type of image consists only of black and white pixels?
questions.why: A binary image has only two values, 0 (black) and 1 (white), one bit per pixel. A greyscale image also has the levels in between.
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model2-7 · solved here

questions.text: What happens when the bit depth of a grayscale image increases?
options: The number of possible gray levels decreases
The number of gray levels increases, improving image detail
questions.why: k bits give `2^k` grey levels (1 bit: 2, 8 bits: 256), so finer brightness changes can be shown. The file gets larger, not smaller.
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model2-8 · solved here

questions.text: Increasing bit depth in grayscale images ......
questions.why: More grey levels means smaller steps between neighbouring tones, so smooth gradients such as a sky no longer break into visible bands (false contouring).
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model2-9 · solved here

questions.text: Piecewise Linear Transformation function involves which of the following?
questions.why: Contrast stretching, intensity-level slicing and bit-plane slicing are the three piecewise-linear transformation functions in Gonzalez and Woods. The course slides and book show only contrast stretching under this heading, so the two slicing methods come from Gonzalez and Woods. The platform shuffled these options but kept their original letters A–D in the text, so they are shown here in that A–D order.
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model3-1 · solved here

questions.text: Expanding a mean filter from 3×3 to 7×7 will ......
questions.why: Each output becomes the average of 49 pixels instead of 9, so noise and detail are smoothed (blurred) more, and the computation grows.
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model3-2 · solved here

questions.text: In digital imaging, brightness values range from ......
questions.why: In the usual 8-bit greyscale image there are `2^8 = 256` levels, from 0 (black) to 255 (white).
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model3-3 · solved here

questions.text: The Sobel operator uses how many kernels?
questions.why: One 3×3 mask for the horizontal change (Gx, finds vertical edges) and one for the vertical change (Gy, finds horizontal edges); the edge strength is `√(Gx² + Gy²)`.
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model3-5 · solved here

questions.text: Piecewise linear transformation provides flexibility for mapping intensity ranges.
questions.why: Each straight segment maps one input range to a chosen output range, so ranges can be stretched, compressed or highlighted at will.
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model3-7 · solved here

questions.text: What is the main characteristic of point processing operations?
options: They transform the image into the frequency domain
They modify each pixel based on its neighboring pixels
They depend on the entire image structure
They modify each pixel independently of other pixels
questions.why: A point operation is `y = f(x)`: the new value depends only on the pixel's own old value. Using neighbours is neighbourhood processing, and using the whole image is transform processing.
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model3-8 · solved here

questions.text: Replication padding replaces edge pixels with the nearest border value.
questions.why: With replicate padding, every pixel added outside the border copies the value of the nearest border pixel (MATLAB's 'replicate'), unlike zero padding.
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model3-9 · solved here

questions.text: Neighborhood processing is slower than point processing.
questions.why: A point operation is one lookup per pixel, while a 3×3 neighbourhood needs 9 multiplications and additions per pixel (49 for 7×7).
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model4 · solved here

questions.text: Bit depth determines ......
options: Number of possible gray levels or colors
questions.why: k bits per pixel give `2^k` possible values (grey levels, or colours in a colour image). It also affects the file size, but not only that.
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model4 · solved here

questions.text: Transform processing operates on ......
questions.why: Transform processing (for example the Fourier transform) treats the whole image as one large block: transform, process, inverse transform. Local regions and pixel groups are neighbourhood processing.
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model4 · solved here

questions.text: Gamma correction with γ < 1 makes an image darker.
questions.why: False: with `s = c·r^γ` on a 0–1 scale, γ < 1 lifts the dark values, so the image becomes brighter (64 → 128 for γ = 0.5 on 0–255); γ > 1 makes it darker.
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model7-8 · solved here

questions.text: The sum of coefficients in a Laplacian filter is ......
questions.why: For example `[0 1 0; 1 −4 1; 0 1 0]` adds up to 0, so a flat region gives 0 and only intensity changes (edges) respond: it is a high-pass mask.
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model4 · solved here

questions.text: Median filter replaces pixel values with the average of neighbors.
questions.why: False: it replaces each pixel by the median (the middle value of the sorted neighbourhood), which is why it removes salt-and-pepper noise. Replacing by the average is the mean filter.
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model5 · solved here

questions.text: Removing noise from an image is part of ......
questions.why: Pre-processing improves the image before the main job: removing noise, enhancing contrast, smoothing or sharpening. Segmentation, feature extraction and recognition come after it.
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model5 · solved here

questions.text: Which statement correctly differentiates image processing from computer vision?
options: Image processing extracts knowledge, computer vision enhances images
Image processing enhances and analyzes images, while computer vision interprets and understands them
Image processing focuses on hardware design while computer vision deals with photography
There is no difference between them
questions.why: Image processing takes an image in and gives an improved image or measurements out; computer vision goes further and interprets the scene, like the brain after the eye. The first option swaps the two.
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model7-1 · solved here

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT an example of a point processing operation?
questions.why: Gaussian smoothing is a weighted average over a neighbourhood. Thresholding, histogram equalization and brightness adjustment map each grey level through a function of that value alone.
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model5 · solved here

questions.text: In convolution, the sum of filter coefficients of a mean filter equals ......
questions.why: A 3×3 mean mask has nine coefficients of 1/9, and 9 × 1/9 = 1, so a flat region keeps its brightness. 9 is only the number of coefficients (their sum before dividing by 9), and 0 is the sum of a high-pass mask.
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model7-2 · solved here

questions.text: Convolution combines the filter and image pixels using a ......
questions.why: Each output is `Σ w(s, t)·f(x − s, y − t)`: the neighbours multiplied by the mask coefficients and added up. Taking the median is a non-linear filter, not convolution.
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model7-6 · solved here

questions.text: Which transformation function produces a photographic negative effect?
questions.why: `s = L − 1 − r` reverses the grey scale (for 8 bits, 0 ↔ 255), so dark becomes light like a photographic negative.
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model6 · solved here

questions.text: Histogram represents:
options: The color composition of an image
The frequency of each gray level in an image
The time variation of pixel intensity
questions.why: The histogram gives n_k, the number of pixels at each grey level k. It says nothing about where those pixels are.
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model7-3 · solved here

questions.text: High-boost filtering enhances image details by amplifying the high-frequency components.
questions.why: `f_hb = A·f − blur = (A − 1)·f + (f − blur)`: the high-pass part (edges and detail) is added on top of a scaled copy of the original, so detail is emphasized while the background is kept.
questions.ref: Platform Quiz 1 2025 · Q model7-5 · solved here

questions.text: What does each point in the frequency domain represent?
options: A frequency component of the spatial image
questions.why: Each F(u, v) is the amount (magnitude and phase) of one sinusoid of frequency (u, v) in the image; low frequencies describe smooth areas and high frequencies edges and detail. It is not tied to any one pixel.

questions.text: The cutoff frequency D₀ controls:
questions.why: D₀ is the radius of the pass region. In a low-pass filter a smaller D₀ removes more frequencies and blurs more, a larger D₀ keeps more detail, so it sets how smooth (or, for a high-pass filter, how sharp) the result is.

questions.text: Filtering in the frequency domain is often:
questions.why: Spatial convolution costs grow with the mask size, while FFT, multiply and inverse FFT cost about the same for any filter size, so for large filters the frequency domain is more efficient.

questions.text: Laplacian filter detects regions with slow intensity change.
questions.why: False: the Laplacian is a second-derivative (high-pass) mask whose coefficients add up to 0, so flat or slowly changing regions give about 0. It responds to rapid intensity changes such as edges, lines and points.

questions.text: The DC component appears in the Fourier spectrum at:
questions.why: Convention-dependent. The DC term F(0, 0) is computed at the origin, so in an unshifted spectrum (raw `fft2`) it is at the top-left corner; spectra are displayed and filtered after `fftshift` (or multiplying by `(−1)^(x+y)`), which moves it to the centre (M/2, N/2). The answer Center assumes the usual centred display; for a raw transform it is Top-left.

questions.text: Zero padding in spatial filtering refers to:
options: Setting missing edge pixels to zero
Replacing all pixel values with zeros
questions.why: When the mask hangs over the border, the missing neighbours outside the image are taken as 0. Ignoring the border pixels is the no-padding option, which shrinks the output.

questions.text: Q1.1: The transformation `g(x,y) = a·f(x,y) + b` is used for: ......
questions.why: It is a linear point operation: the gain a scales the grey levels (contrast) and the offset b shifts them (brightness).

questions.text: Q1.3: Increasing D₀ in a low-pass filter makes the image: ......
questions.why: D₀ is the cutoff radius. A larger D₀ lets more high frequencies through, so less detail is removed and the result is sharper (closer to the original); a smaller D₀ blurs more.

questions.text: Q1.4: Ideal filters cause ringing because: ......
questions.why: The ideal filter jumps from 1 to 0 at D₀; that sharp cutoff corresponds to a sinc-like spatial kernel with ripples, which appear as rings around edges. Butterworth and Gaussian filters roll off smoothly and ring less or not at all.

questions.text: Q1.5: Which domain uses convolution to apply filters?
questions.why: In the spatial domain a filter is applied by convolving the image with a mask; by the convolution theorem the frequency domain does the same thing by multiplication.

questions.text: Q1.6: Frequency domain filtering involves operations performed on: ......
questions.why: The steps are: take the DFT of the image, multiply it by the filter H(u, v), and take the inverse DFT; the filter acts on the Fourier transform, not on the pixels.

questions.text: Q1.8: Which of the following noise types is most effectively reduced by a median filter?
questions.why: Salt-and-pepper impulses are extreme values that end up at the ends of the sorted window, so the median never picks them; averaging-type noise such as Gaussian noise is better handled by mean filters.

questions.text: Q1.9: High-boost filtering enhances ......
questions.why: High-boost adds the high-pass (edge and detail) image to A − 1 times the original, so edges and fine detail are emphasised while the overall image is kept.

questions.text: Q1.10: Histogram equalization redistributes pixel intensities to achieve a ......
questions.why: Equalization maps each level through the scaled cumulative histogram so that, ideally, every grey level occurs equally often: a flat (uniform) histogram, achieved only approximately for digital images.

questions.text: Q1.11: Which of the following causes image degradation?
questions.why: Motion blur and noise damage the image, and restoration tries to recover the degraded original (L1 aspects of image processing; book Ch 1 p. 26: noise removal, deblurring). Illumination adjustment, histogram equalization and gamma correction are enhancement operations applied on purpose.

questions.text: Q1.12: Convolution combines: ......
options: Kernel weights and neighboring pixel values
questions.why: Each output pixel is the sum of the kernel weights multiplied by the pixel values under the (rotated) kernel.

questions.text: Q1.13: Adding Laplacian output to original image produces: ......
questions.why: Combining the Laplacian's edge information with the original sharpens the image (with the negative-centre mask it is subtracted, g = f − ∇²f; with the positive-centre mask it is added).

questions.text: Q1.14: Padding is used to: ......
questions.why: At the border part of the mask falls outside the image; padding (zeros, replicate, mirror, wrap) supplies those missing neighbours so the output keeps the input size.

questions.text: Q1.15: Increasing resolution generally results in ......
questions.why: More pixels per unit length sample the scene more finely, so more detail is captured (and the file gets larger).

questions.text: Q2.1: The goal of restoration is to make an image look subjectively better to the human eye.
questions.why: False: that is enhancement, which is subjective. Restoration is objective: it models the degradation (blur, noise) and tries to recover the original image.

questions.text: Q2.3: Point processing modifies each pixel using information from its neighboring pixels.
questions.why: False: point processing uses only the pixel's own value, y = f(x); using the neighbours is neighbourhood processing (spatial filtering).

questions.text: Q2.4: Contrast stretching enhances details by expanding intensity range.
questions.why: Stretching spreads the occupied grey levels over a wider range, so neighbouring levels become easier to tell apart.

questions.text: Q2.5: Image segmentation is performed before image acquisition in the processing pipeline.
questions.why: False: acquisition always comes first; segmentation is done after acquisition and preprocessing, before representation and recognition.

questions.text: Q2.6: The Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) is only used for 1D signals.
questions.why: False: the 2-D DFT of an image is computed with the FFT, applied to the rows and then the columns, which is how frequency-domain image filtering is done in practice.

questions.text: Q2.7: A high-pass filter enhances the low-frequency components of an image.
questions.why: False: a high-pass filter keeps and emphasises the high-frequency components (edges, fine detail) and attenuates the low frequencies (smooth regions).

questions.text: Q2.8: Binary images are primarily used for applications like document scanning and segmentation.
questions.why: With one bit per pixel, binary images suit text and document scanning, fingerprints and plans, and they are the usual output of thresholding/segmentation (masks).

questions.text: Q2.9: For edge detection we use the first derivative and third derivative.
questions.why: False: edge detection uses the first derivative (the gradient, e.g. the Sobel masks) and the second derivative (the Laplacian), not the third (book Ch 3 pp. 72–77).

questions.text: Q2.10: Image restoration techniques can handle motion blur.
questions.why: Restoration reverses damage done to an image by a known cause, and removing the blur caused by linear (camera) motion is the standard example (L1 slide 49, aspects of image processing).

questions.text: Q4c: Mention some important applications of image processing.

steps.text: Medical imaging: enhancing X-ray, CT and MRI images, detecting tumours, measuring organs, classifying chest X-rays (e.g. for COVID-19).
Surveillance (CCTV): real-time monitoring, counting people, detecting crowds and abnormal behaviour.
Traffic: automatic number plate recognition (ANPR) for gates, tolls and vehicle tracking.
Self-driving cars and robots: detecting lanes, traffic lights, signs and obstacles, even in fog.
Industrial inspection: checking and sorting products, rejecting faulty or unlabelled items on a conveyor belt.
Remote sensing and astronomy: enhancing satellite and telescope images for maps, weather, crops and land use.
Documents and biometrics: scanning and reading text (OCR), fingerprint, iris and face recognition.
Photography and media: removing noise, sharpening, adjusting brightness, contrast and colour, compressing images for storage and transmission.

questions.text: MCQ 8: The operation of edge detection that calculates the gradient magnitude is:
questions.why: Prewitt and Sobel are both first-derivative (gradient) operators: two directional masks give Gx and Gy and the edge strength is the gradient magnitude. The Laplacian is a second derivative and has no gradient direction.

questions.text: MCQ 9: Which of the following is used to resolve the dark features in the image?
questions.why: A power-law (gamma) transformation with γ < 1 expands the dark grey levels and brightens the image, revealing detail in dark regions (the same question as the Nov 2023 midterm, Q1.1).

questions.text: MCQ 10: Sobel edge detection uses ...... Derivative.
questions.why: Sobel is a first-order derivative (gradient) operator that also smooths slightly; the Laplacian is the second-derivative operator.

questions.text: Q3a, step 1 of 2: what is the first derivative `f(x + 1) − f(x)` of the profile 50 50 60 90 100 100 100?
questions.why: Differences of neighbours: 50 − 50 = 0, 60 − 50 = 10, 90 − 60 = 30, 100 − 90 = 10, 0, 0. The negated list uses f(x) − f(x + 1), and 10 20 −20 −10 0 is the second derivative.
questions.ref: Final (year unknown) · Q3a step 1 · solved here

questions.text: Q3a, step 2 of 2: what is the second derivative `f(x + 1) + f(x − 1) − 2f(x)` at the interior samples of 50 50 60 90 100 100 100?
questions.why: x = 1: 60 + 50 − 100 = 10; x = 2: 90 + 50 − 120 = 20; x = 3: 100 + 60 − 180 = −20; x = 4: 100 + 90 − 200 = −10; x = 5: 0. The sign change between 20 and −20 is the zero crossing of the edge.
questions.ref: Final (year unknown) · Q3a step 2 · solved here

questions.text: Q3a: Find the first derivative and the second derivative of the following sub-image (a 1-D profile): f = 50 50 60 90 100 100 100.

steps.text: First derivative (forward difference): `∂f/∂x = f(x + 1) − f(x)`; it is defined for x = 0..5.
Second derivative: `∂²f/∂x² = f(x + 1) + f(x − 1) − 2f(x)`, the 1-D form of the Laplacian; it is defined for the interior samples x = 1..5.
Compute both at every position (– = not defined).
The first derivative is non-zero all along the ramp 50 → 100 (a thick response) and 0 in the flat parts.

The second derivative gives a double response, + at the start of the ramp and − at its end, with a zero crossing between 60 and 90 that locates the edge; it is 0 in flat regions and along a constant slope.

questions.why: The first derivative uses the forward difference f(x + 1) − f(x) (Gonzalez and Woods); a backward difference gives the same numbers shifted by one position.

questions.text: Q3b, step 1 of 1: stretching the image (values 1 to 20) to [0, 255], what does the pixel 12 become?
questions.why: s = (r − r_min) × 255 / (r_max − r_min) = (12 − 1) × 255 / 19 = 147.6 → 148. 147 truncates instead of rounding, 153 is 12 × 255 / 20 (no minimum subtracted), and 161 is 12 × 255 / 19.
questions.ref: Final (year unknown) · Q3b step 1 · solved here

questions.text: Q3b: Apply contrast stretching to the following image to stretch it to the new range [0, 255]. (The pixels 12 and 15 are circled on the paper.)

steps.text: The occupied range is r_min = 1 to r_max = 20, so `s = (r − 1) × 255 / 19`, rounded to the nearest integer.
Compute every pixel.
Put the values back in place.
The minimum 1 becomes 0 and the maximum 20 becomes 255; the steps between values grow by the factor 255 / 19 ≈ 13.4.
The circled pixels: 12 → 148 and 15 → 188.

questions.text: Q3c: Give a short description of the types of digital images.

steps.text: Binary image: each pixel is 0 (black) or 1 (white), 1 bit per pixel; used for text, fingerprints, plans, and as the output of thresholding and edge detection.
Grayscale image: each pixel is a shade of grey, usually 0 (black) to 255 (white), 8 bits per pixel; used for X-rays, printed photos and most image processing.
True colour (RGB) image: each pixel has red, green and blue values, 0–255 each, so 24 bits per pixel (16,777,216 colours); stored as three matrices; used for photographs.
Indexed image: each pixel stores an index into a colour map (palette) of up to 256 colours, 8 bits per pixel plus the small map; used for GIFs, icons and cartoons.

questions.text: Q5a, step 1 of 2: in the 3-bit 3×4 image below, what does grey level 6 map to after histogram equalization?

questions.text: The process of moving a filter mask over the image and computing the sum of products at each location is defined by ......
questions.why: Laying the mask directly on the image and adding the products at each position is correlation; this sentence is Gonzalez and Woods' definition of it, and the site's L3 page says the same. Convolution does the same after rotating the mask by 180°. Convention: the course book (p. 59) writes this un-rotated sum `g(x, y) = Σ Σ w(s, t)·f(x + s, y + t)` under the name convolution, so a key based on the book could accept Convolution.

questions.text: The sum of all components of a normalised histogram is equal to ......
options: Size of rows of the image
Size of columns of the image
questions.why: The normalised histogram is p(r_k) = n_k / MN, so its components add up to MN / MN = 1. The unnormalised counts n_k add up to M×N.

questions.text: Convolution is usually used in the ...... domain.
questions.why: Convolving the image with a mask is the spatial-domain filtering operation; in the frequency domain it becomes a multiplication (convolution theorem).

questions.text: Fourier transform is a ...... transform
questions.why: The transform of a·f + b·g is a·F + b·G (the linearity property of the DFT). Bilinear and bicubic are interpolation methods, not transforms.

questions.text: Ideal filters can be ......
questions.why: An ideal filter is a sharp 0/1 cutoff at D₀: it can keep the low frequencies (ILPF), the high frequencies (IHPF = 1 − ILPF), or a band between two cutoffs (band-pass).

questions.text: Which of the following filters is effective in the presence of salt-and-pepper noise?
questions.why: Salt-and-pepper pixels are extreme values that sort to the ends of the window, so the median ignores them. The average smears them over the neighbourhood, and Sobel and Roberts are edge detectors.

questions.text: An image element is usually called a ......
questions.why: The elements of a digital image are called picture elements, image elements, pels or pixels, and pixel is the term used most widely (L1 slide 38); f(x, y) is the value at an element, not its name. The paper's intent is unclear: a key could accept All of the above by reading picture point and f(x,y) loosely.

questions.text: Q2b: Briefly explain the operation of the Alpha-trimmed mean filter. What are its uses for image processing?

steps.text: Slide a window (for example 3×3) over the image and sort the values under it.
Trim (delete) the same number of values, d/2, from each end of the sorted list: the lowest and the highest values.
Replace the centre pixel by the mean of the values that remain; for 3×3 with two trimmed at each end: `(x3 + x4 + x5 + x6 + x7) / 5`.
Example: sorted 1 4 5 7 8 10 12 15 70 → keep 5 7 8 10 12 → 42 / 5 = 8.4 (the mean would be 14.67, the median 8).
It is a non-linear (order-statistic) filter between the mean (d = 0) and the median (trim all but the middle value).
Uses: smoothing images with mixed noise, such as salt-and-pepper plus Gaussian noise; trimming removes the impulses and averaging the rest smooths the Gaussian part.

questions.text: Q3a: List the major steps needed for performing edge detection of an image by thresholding the gradient magnitude computed using the Sobel operator. For simplicity, assume the threshold value is given in advance, denoted by T.

steps.text: Read the image and convert it to a greyscale array of doubles, so that negative derivative values are not clipped.
Filter the image with the Sobel mask `Gx = [−1 0 1; −2 0 2; −1 0 1]` (sum of products at each pixel); Gx responds to vertical edges.
Filter the image with the Sobel mask `Gy = [−1 −2 −1; 0 0 0; 1 2 1]`; Gy responds to horizontal edges.
At every pixel compute the gradient magnitude `M(x, y) = √(Gx² + Gy²)` (often approximated by `|Gx| + |Gy|`).
Threshold the magnitude: `E(x, y) = 1` (edge) if `M(x, y) ≥ T`, otherwise `E(x, y) = 0`.
The result E is a binary edge map; the edge direction, if needed, is `θ = tan⁻¹(Gy / Gx)`.

questions.why: Sobel, the two masks and the gradient magnitude are in the course book's Sobel section (Ch 3, pp. 75–76); comparing each value with a given T is the thresholding point operation of L1–L2. Choosing T automatically (Otsu, adaptive) would be Lecture 9, but the paper gives T.

questions.text: Q3b: Write a MATLAB function that implements the steps in (a), assuming the image size is W (width) × H (height). You can ignore the boundary problem by performing edge detection only on non-boundary pixels.

steps.text: Function header, with the image f and the threshold T as inputs: `function E = sobel_edge(f, T)`
Convert to double, read the size (rows = H, columns = W) and start with an all-zero edge map: `f = double(f); [H, W] = size(f); E = zeros(H, W);`
Visit only the non-boundary pixels: `for r = 2:H-1, for c = 2:W-1`
Take the 3×3 neighbourhood of the pixel: `w = f(r-1:r+1, c-1:c+1);`
Sum of products with each mask: `gx = sum(sum(Gx .* w)); gy = sum(sum(Gy .* w));`
Mark an edge where the gradient magnitude reaches T: `if sqrt(gx^2 + gy^2) >= T, E(r, c) = 1; end`
Close both loops and the function: `end, end, end`

questions.why: Any correct loop version is fine; the masks may also be applied with `conv2` or `imfilter` and the magnitude thresholded in one line, `E = sqrt(gx.^2 + gy.^2) >= T`, but the paper asks for the boundary pixels to be skipped, which the loops from 2 to H−1 and 2 to W−1 do.
